opus-5.5.text:
I think it applies in a really interesting way, partly because a lot of that older work is being rediscovered almost by accident. There was a long tradition in HCI, going back to the debates about direct manipulation versus command lines in the eighties, of asking very carefully: what is a picture good for, and what is language good for? And the answer was never "pictures are better" or "text is better." It was that they have different strengths. Graphics are wonderful when you want people to see many things at once, to compare, to notice patterns, to perceive structure in parallel. Text, and language more broadly, is wonderful when you need to express something abstract, something compositional, something like "all the files modified last Tuesday except the ones in this folder." Try doing that by pointing and clicking.

What's happened with large language models is that, suddenly, the pendulum has swung very hard toward language. The chat box is the interface for almost everything. And I think the older research would gently remind us that a chat box is a pretty narrow channel. It's serial. You read one thing, then the next thing. If the system knows a lot about some complex situation, squeezing all of that through a stream of tokens is not always the best way to help a person understand it. That's exactly the kind of case where visualization earned its place.

So my hope, and what I think the history suggests, is that we'll end up with hybrid interfaces. Language is fantastic for expressing intent: "show me how these customers differ," say. But the response often shouldn't just be a paragraph; it might be a chart, or an interactive view you can manipulate directly, with language available again when you want to refine things. Some of the best ideas from the direct manipulation era, like immediate feedback, reversible actions, and seeing the state of the system, still matter a lot. One of the frustrations with pure chat interfaces is that you often can't see the state. You don't know what the system thinks, what it's assuming, what it's going to do.

And that connects to something I care about from the interpretability side. If we can understand some of the internal representations of these models, for instance what the model believes about the user, or about the task, then that's something you might want to display graphically, as a kind of dashboard, rather than asking the model to describe itself in words, which may or may not be faithful. So in a funny way, the old question of when to use graphics versus text comes back at a new level: not just how to show the data, but how to show the system itself.

r001.rationale: The response explains that graphics and language have different strengths and gives examples of older HCI ideas that still matter. It does not clearly identify uncertainty about which established intuitions remain valid for modern interfaces.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think about this a lot, because there's this wonderful body of work from the eighties and nineties that people have sort of forgotten about. Ben Shneiderman, Stuart Card, Jock Mackinlay, Bill Cleveland's perceptual research on how accurately people read different visual encodings. And the striking thing is that the core findings haven't aged at all, because they're really about human perception and cognition, not about any particular technology.

The basic lesson was something like: graphics are great when you want someone to see a pattern, a comparison, an outlier, a shape in the data. Position and length are the encodings people read most precisely. Text is great when you need exactness, when you need to name things, when the content is inherently discrete or categorical, or when you need to convey nuance that doesn't reduce to a number. And the mistake people made then, and still make now, is treating a chart as decoration rather than as an argument. If there's no pattern to see, you don't need a picture.

What I find interesting about today's interfaces is that the question has gotten more complicated in a couple of ways. One is that a lot of what we interact with now is language, especially with large language models. The interface is a text box. And I think there's a real temptation to say, well, text is the universal interface now, we can just talk to everything. I don't believe that. If I ask a model to compare twenty things along five dimensions, reading a paragraph about it is a terrible experience. I want a table, or a chart, or something I can scan. So the old HCI question of "when do you reach for a graphical element" is actually more pressing, because now the system has to make that decision on the fly, for every response, rather than a designer making it once.

The other shift is that the old work mostly assumed a human was looking at a fixed artifact. Today a lot of the interesting visualization work I do is about looking inside these models, and there the graphical element isn't just presenting data, it's a way of forming a hypothesis you couldn't have articulated in words yet. Looking at an attention pattern or an embedding projection, you often see something before you can say what it is. That was always true of good visualization, going back to Tukey, but I think it's a part of the old research that's underappreciated in the current moment. Everyone is focused on the output side, and the exploratory side, where the picture comes before the sentence, is where I'd love to see more people applying those classic ideas.

r001.rationale: The response asserts that the classic findings remain valid and explains how they apply today. It does not identify uncertainty about which established intuitions still hold.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of that research is still relevant, because the basic question is: what is somebody trying to do? If you want to see a pattern, spot an outlier, or compare a lot of things at once, a graphical representation can be incredibly useful. If you want an exact value, or an explanation with qualifications, text may be much better.

And often the interesting answer is to combine them. A chart can show you something surprising, and a little bit of text can help explain why it matters. With conversational interfaces, it’s tempting to make everything a conversation, but asking someone to read three paragraphs to understand a trend that they could see in a second seems like a step backward. The opportunity is to make it easier to move between those representations, depending on what the person needs.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier research is still relevant and describes when graphics or text help, but it does not identify uncertainty about which established designer or HCI intuitions remain valid for modern interfaces.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic question still applies, but I’d be careful about turning it into a rule that graphics are better than text, or vice versa. It depends on what somebody is trying to do. If you want an exact value, a sentence or a little table may be perfect. If you want to see a trend, an outlier, or a relationship among lots of things, a graphic can make that immediately apparent.

What’s interesting about today’s interfaces is that we have more opportunities to combine them. You might start with a visualization, ask a question in language, and get an explanation that points back to something in the picture. Those representations can support each other.

So I’d take the earlier HCI work as a way of asking good questions: What’s the task? What does the person already know? What do they need to compare or remember? Then you still have to test whether the interface actually helps. The fact that we can generate a beautiful graphic—or a very fluent paragraph—doesn’t tell us that it’s the right representation.

r001.rationale: The response treats earlier HCI intuitions as conditional rather than settled rules: the right representation depends on the task, and whether an interface helps must be tested.
